claim: Standard treatment for metastatic prostate cancer prevents ligand-activation of androgen receptor (AR).
source: Standard treatment for metastatic prostate cancer (CaP) prevents ligand-activation of androgen receptor (AR).
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice in prostate cancer treatment, representing established medical knowledge.

claim: Despite initial remission, CaP progresses while relying on AR.
source: Despite initial remission, CaP progresses while relying on AR.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the Introduction section referencing established literature on ADT resistance.

claim: In a 452-AR-target gene panel, each of 18 clinically relevant coregulators mediates androgen-responsiveness of 0–57% genes.
source: In a 452-AR-target gene panel, each of 18 clinically relevant coregulators mediates androgen-responsiveness of 0–57% genes and acts as a coactivator or corepressor in a gene-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from oligoarray analyses shown in Figure 1B and described in the Results section.

claim: Each of 18 clinically relevant coregulators acts as a coactivator or corepressor in a gene-specific manner.
source: In a 452-AR-target gene panel, each of 18 clinically relevant coregulators mediates androgen-responsiveness of 0–57% genes and acts as a coactivator or corepressor in a gene-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that coregulators can both increase and decrease androgen-responsiveness of different genes, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WDR77 unites the actions of AR and p53 to control cell cycle progression.
source: Isolation of a novel transcriptional mechanism in which WDR77 unites the actions of AR and p53, the major genomic drivers of lethal CaP, to control cell cycle progression provides proof-of-principle for treatment via selective interference with AR action by exploiting AR dependence on coregulators.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental data including Co-IP studies (Figure 3B-E), gene expression analyses (Figure 3F), and cell cycle analyses (Figure 6E).

claim: AR and p53 are the major genomic drivers of lethal CaP.
source: Isolation of a novel transcriptional mechanism in which WDR77 unites the actions of AR and p53, the major genomic drivers of lethal CaP, to control cell cycle progression provides proof-of-principle for treatment via selective interference with AR action by exploiting AR dependence on coregulators.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature (Robinson et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2015) mentioned in the Results section.

claim: Failure of ADT is responsible for ~27,000 CaP deaths in the United States annually.
source: With few exceptions, failure of ADT is responsible for the ~27,000 CaP deaths in the United States annually (Siegel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to epidemiological data from Siegel et al., 2017.

claim: AR's effector function as a transcription factor controls expression of Androgen Response Element (ARE)-driven genes.
source: AR's effector function as a transcription factor controls expression of Androgen Response Element (ARE)-driven genes (Heinlein and Chang, 2004; Heemers and Tindall, 2007) and ultimately dictates androgen-regulated CaP cell behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on AR function.

claim: AR's transcriptional function ultimately dictates androgen-regulated CaP cell behavior.
source: AR's effector function as a transcription factor controls expression of Androgen Response Element (ARE)-driven genes (Heinlein and Chang, 2004; Heemers and Tindall, 2007) and ultimately dictates androgen-regulated CaP cell behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established role of AR as a transcription factor and its control over gene expression.

claim: Expression of 50 of the ~200 AR-associated coregulators is deregulated in clinical CaP specimens.
source: Expression of 50 of the ~200 AR-associated coregulators is deregulated in clinical CaP specimens.
evidence: This statement is based on a review of literature as indicated by the context and citations in the Introduction.

claim: Aberrant expression of coregulators often correlates with aggressive disease and poor outcome.
source: Such aberrant expression often correlates with aggressive disease and poor outcome (Heemers and Tindall, 2010) and is one of the mechanisms that lead to resistance to conventional ADT.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heemers and Tindall, 2010.

claim: Aberrant coregulator expression is one of the mechanisms that lead to resistance to conventional ADT.
source: Such aberrant expression often correlates with aggressive disease and poor outcome (Heemers and Tindall, 2010) and is one of the mechanisms that lead to resistance to conventional ADT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between coregulator expression and disease progression, supported by citation.

claim: ARBSs present within 300 Kb of TSSs of RefSeq genes after androgen treatment were retrieved from LNCaP cells.
source: ARBSs present within 300 Kb of TSSs of RefSeq genes after androgen treatment (Wang et al., 2009) of AR-positive LNCaP cells were retrieved, and the overlap between the corresponding RefSeq gene list and androgen-dependent CaP gene expression profiles (Wang et al., 2009; DePrimo et al., 2002; Nelson et al., 2002; Segawa et al., 2002; Febbo et al., 2005; Velasco et al., 2004; Ngan et al., 2009; Waghray et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2001) was defined.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, based on data from Wang et al., 2009.

claim: Integration of ARBS location, TSS position, and androgen-responsive gene expression narrowed down a set of 12,629 ARBSs to 900 putative direct AR target genes.
source: This approach narrowed down a set of 12,629 ARBSs to 900 putative direct AR target genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental approach described and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oligoarray data revealed 452 genes with at least 2-fold change in expression in response to androgens.
source: Oligoarray data revealed 452 genes with at least 2-fold change in expression in response to androgens (Supplementary file 1, panel B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental oligoarray data.

claim: Androgen treatment increased expression of 241 (55%) of the 452 genes.
source: Androgen treatment increased expression of 241 (55%) of these genes, while reducing expression of the remaining 211.
evidence: This is supported by oligoarray expression data.

claim: Androgen treatment reduced expression of 211 of the 452 genes.
source: Androgen treatment increased expression of 241 (55%) of these genes, while reducing expression of the remaining 211.
evidence: This is supported by oligoarray expression data.

claim: Androgen dependence and directionality of androgen regulation of >90% of the genes were also present in VCaP cells.
source: Androgen dependence and directionality of androgen regulation of >90% of the genes were also present in an independent AR-positive cell line, VCaP (Korenchuk et al., 2001) (Supplementary file 2, panel A, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation in VCaP cells.

claim: The kinetics of androgen response was consistent with behavior of direct AR target genes, with androgen-induction notable at earlier time points (4 hr) than androgen-suppression (8 hr).
source: The kinetics of androgen response (Supplementary file 2, panel B) was consistent with behavior of direct AR target genes, that is, androgen-induction of genes was notable at earlier time points (4 hr) than androgen-suppression (8 hr).
evidence: This is supported by time course experimental data.

claim: ChIP verified androgen-dependent recruitment of AR to predicted AREs within ARBSs.
source: ChIP verified androgen-dependent recruitment of AR to predicted AREs within ARBSs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARBSs were predominantly located in enhancer regions and intergenic regions.
source: No preference for particular chromosomes was noted, but consistent with other reports (Horie-Inoue and Inoue, 2013), ARBSs were predominantly located in enhancer regions and intergenic regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: 84.6% of ARBSs in the 452-AR target genes overlapped with androgen-induced H3K4me2 ChIP-Seq peaks.
source: The vast majority (84.6%) of ARBSs in the 452-AR target genes overlapped with androgen-induced H3K4me2 ChIP-Seq peaks, an epigenetic marker for active AR-dependent transcription (He et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published H3K4me2 ChIP-Seq data.

claim: H3K4me2 is an epigenetic marker for active AR-dependent transcription.
source: The vast majority (84.6%) of ARBSs in the 452-AR target genes overlapped with androgen-induced H3K4me2 ChIP-Seq peaks, an epigenetic marker for active AR-dependent transcription (He et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to He et al., 2010.

claim: Cistrome motif analyses of DNA sequences corresponding to ARBSs demonstrated significant enrichment for the consensus AR binding motif.
source: Cistrome motif analyses (Liu et al., 2011) of the DNA sequences that correspond to ARBSs demonstrated significant enrichment for the consensus AR binding motif.
evidence: This is supported by computational cistrome analysis of ARBS sequences.

claim: The top 10 enriched motifs in ARBSs included binding motifs for glucocorticoid and progesterone nuclear receptors, FoxA1, FoxA2, GTF2A1, and STAT1.
source: The top 10 enriched motifs also included the highly similar and sometimes interchangeable binding motifs for related glucocorticoid and progesterone nuclear receptors, as well as AR-interacting pioneering factor FoxA1 and the related FoxA2, general transcription factor GTF2A1 and transcription factors (TFs) such as STAT1 that are known to interact with ARE-bound AR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cistrome motif analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IPA indicated significant enrichment for cell functions associated with cancer, cell growth, cell death and movement, and lipid metabolism in the 452 gene signature.
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (Krämer et al., 2014) (IPA) indicated significant enrichment for cell functions associated with cancer; cell growth (specifically of CaP cells), death and movement, lipid metabolism (Supplementary file 3, panel A).
evidence: This is supported by IPA computational analysis of the gene signature.

claim: Cell growth, death, movement, and lipid metabolism have been independently reported to be under androgen control in CaP cells.
source: These processes have been independently reported to be under androgen control in CaP cells (Dehm and Tindall, 2006; Heemers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At the onset of this study, 181 coregulators that interact physically and functionally with AR had been identified.
source: At the onset of this study, 181 coregulators that interact physically and functionally with AR had been identified (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on a literature review compiled in Supplementary file 1.

claim: For 51 AR-associated coregulators, protein expression was deregulated between CaP and benign prostate.
source: For 51 AR-associated coregulators protein expression was deregulated between CaP and benign prostate.
evidence: This is based on literature review and previous studies.

claim: Differential expression of 22 of the 51 coregulators correlated with more aggressive CaP features and shorter disease-free survival after prostatectomy.
source: Differential expression of 22 of these 51 correlated with more aggressive CaP features and shorter disease-free survival after prostatectomy (Heemers and Tindall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heemers and Tindall, 2010.

claim: Silencing of GAK, HIP1, RAD9A or SMAD3 decreased markedly AR protein expression.
source: Silencing of GAK, HIP1, RAD9A or SMAD3, however, did decrease markedly AR protein expression (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental siRNA knockdown data.

claim: The fraction of genes affected by coregulator silencing varied widely among different coregulators, ranging from 0% for RCHY1 to 57% for p300.
source: The fraction of genes affected varied widely among different coregulators, ranging from 0% for RCHY1 siRNA transfection to 57% (258/452 genes affected) for p300 knock-down.
evidence: This is supported by oligoarray gene expression data after coregulator knockdown, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each coregulator studied could simultaneously increase the androgen-responsiveness of a subset of AR target genes and decrease androgen-responsiveness of other genes.
source: Strikingly, each coregulator studied could simultaneously increase the androgen-responsiveness of a subset of AR target genes under its control (thus acting as a coactivator) and decrease androgen-responsiveness of other genes that rely on it for androgen regulation (acting as corepressor) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Androgen-responsiveness of the same AR target gene could be affected by multiple coregulators.
source: Androgen-responsiveness of the same AR target gene could be affected by multiple coregulators.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of coregulator dependencies shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 5.

claim: 2 to 4 coregulators affected the androgen-responsiveness of the vast majority of genes.
source: 2 to 4 coregulators affected the androgen-responsiveness of the vast majority of genes.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of coregulator dependencies in the data.

claim: Androgen-responsiveness of GNB4 was modified by 4 individual coregulators.
source: For instance, androgen-responsiveness of the genes encoding GNB4 and RAB27A was modified by 4 or 12, respectively, individual coregulators (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Androgen-responsiveness of RAB27A was modified by 12 individual coregulators.
source: For instance, androgen-responsiveness of the genes encoding GNB4 and RAB27A was modified by 4 or 12, respectively, individual coregulators (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: ChIP studies verified the correlation between androgen-dependent recruitment of NCOA3, SMARCA4 or WDR77 to AREs and the pattern of androgen-responsiveness of GNB4 and RAB27A.
source: ChIP studies using antibodies directed against 6 representative coregulators verified the correlation between androgen-dependent recruitment of NCOA3, SMARCA4 or WDR77 to AREs and the pattern of androgen-responsiveness of GNB4 and RAB27A in LNCaP cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experimental data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Coregulators which loss did not affect the androgen regulation of GNB4 and RAB27A, such as PKN1 or NCOA2, were not found at AREs of these genes.
source: Conversely, coregulators which loss did not affect the androgen regulation of these genes, such as PKN1 or NCOA2, were not found at AREs of these genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experimental data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Robust androgen-induced recruitment of AR was seen after 1 hr, 4 hr, or 16 hr at AREs in GNB4 and RAB27A, which became less pronounced or not detectable at 48 hr.
source: Robust androgen-induced recruitment of AR was seen after 1 hr, 4 hr, or 16 hr at AREs in both genes, which became less pronounced (RAB27A) or not detectable (GNB4) at 48 hr.
evidence: This is supported by time course ChIP data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Androgen-stimulated binding of WDR77 and NCOA3 occurred at all time points at AREs of GNB4 and RAB27A.
source: Androgen-stimulated binding of WDR77 and NCOA3 occurred at all time points at AREs of both genes (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by time course ChIP data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Androgen stimulation of GNB4 and RAB27A was first seen at 4 hr.
source: Consistent with a lag between recruitment of AR and changes in androgen responsiveness of its target genes (Massie et al., 2011), androgen stimulation of GNB4 and RAB27A was first seen at 4 hr.
evidence: This is supported by time course gene expression data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: At 16 hr androgen treatment, silencing of both WDR77 and NCOA3 increased the level of androgen regulation of GNB4 and RAB27A.
source: At 16 hr androgen treatment, silencing of both WDR77 and NCOA3 increased the level of androgen regulation of GNB4 as well as RAB27A.
evidence: This is supported by time course gene expression data after coregulator knockdown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The overlap in genes between different coregulator-dependent signatures was less than 30% with few exceptions.
source: With few exceptions (e.g. EP300-BAG1) the overlap in genes between different coregulator-dependent signatures was less than 30%.
evidence: This is supported by pairwise comparison analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Among 136 pair-wise comparisons, only 42 (30.8%) and 31 (22.7%) have significant overlap at the level of p<0.05 and p<0.01, respectively.
source: Among the 136 pair-wise comparisons, only 42 (30.8%) and 31 (22.7%) have significant overlap at the level of p<0.05 and p<0.01, respectively (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of gene set overlaps.

claim: Between STAT3- and WDR77-dependent gene sets, 30 genes overlapped, corresponding to 31% and 28% of gene signatures, respectively.
source: For instance, between STAT3- and WDR77-dependent gene sets, 30 genes overlapped, which corresponds to 31% and 28% of gene signatures, respectively (p=0.99 for significance of this overlap, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by gene set overlap analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The directionality in androgen regulation was preserved for only 15 genes (or 16% and 14%) between STAT3- and WDR77-dependent gene sets.
source: Of note, the directionality in androgen regulation was preserved for only 15 genes (or 16% and 14%) (Figure 1C, insert).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of directionality in overlapping genes shown in Figure 1C insert.

claim: A total of 283 significantly overrepresented TF binding motifs were identified in ARBSs of coregulator-dependent AR target gene signatures.
source: DNA sequences corresponding to ARBSs were retrieved, expanded by 1 kb at the 5' and 3' ends and analyzed using Cistrome Project tools (Liu et al., 2011). A total of 283 significantly overrepresented TF binding motifs were identified (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by cistrome computational analysis.

claim: The number of overrepresented motifs in ARBSs of an individual gene signatures ranged from 4 to 127.
source: The number of overrepresented motifs in ARBSs of an individual gene signatures ranged from 4 to 127 (Figure 2A) and did not correlate with the number of genes per coregulator-dependent gene signature or corresponding number of ARBSs (some genes harbor >1 ARBS).
evidence: This is supported by cistrome analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The predominant motif overrepresented in ARBSs from the 452 gene list and the 17 subgroups was one that matched the binding site for AR.
source: The predominant motif overrepresented in ARBSs from the 452 gene list and the 17 subgroups was one that matched the binding site for AR.
evidence: This is supported by cistrome motif analysis.

claim: Each individual coregulator-dependent AR target gene set harbored in its ARBSs at least one overrepresented TF binding motif that was not found to be overrepresented in ARBSs in other AR target gene lists or in the overarching 452 gene set.
source: Strikingly, however, each individual coregulator-dependent AR target gene set harbored in its ARBSs at least one overrepresented TF binding motif that was not found to be overrepresented in ARBSs in other AR target gene lists or in the overarching 452 gene set (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by cistrome motif analysis shown in Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: Multiple TF binding sites that are enriched selectively in STAT3-dependent gene ARBSs correspond to TFs that function in development, organogenesis and stemness.
source: For instance, multiple TF binding sites that are enriched selectively in STAT3-dependent gene ARBSs but not in other subsignatures correspond to TFs that function in development, organogenesis and stemness (e.g MEIS2, NANOG, SOX2) (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by cistrome analysis and functional annotation of enriched TF binding sites.

claim: The entire 452 AR target gene set was associated with 36 IPA categories.
source: The entire 452 AR target gene set was associated with 36 categories, whereas individual AR target gene signatures were associated with 0 (e.g. CAV1) to 34 (for SMARCA4) categories (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by IPA functional analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Individual AR target gene signatures were associated with 0 to 34 IPA categories.
source: The entire 452 AR target gene set was associated with 36 categories, whereas individual AR target gene signatures were associated with 0 (e.g. CAV1) to 34 (for SMARCA4) categories (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by IPA functional analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SMARCC1-dependent AR target genes associated significantly with functions involved in cell death and survival.
source: For instance, SMARCC1-dependent AR target genes associated significantly with functions involved in cell death and survival.
evidence: This is supported by IPA functional analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Expression of the 452 gene signature was negatively enriched in benign cells from patients who received dutasteride.
source: The expression of the overarching 452 gene signature was negatively enriched in benign cells from patients who received dutasteride, indicating androgen regulation of this gene set in normal benign prostate epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of clinical gene expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: For 4 gene subsignatures (PARK7-, FHL2-, WDR77-, and EP300-dependent), no changes were seen between dutasteride-treated versus vehicle-treated patients, indicating no androgen regulation of these genes in normal benign epithelial prostate cells.
source: For 4 gene subsignatures (PARK7-, FHL2-, WDR77-, and EP300-dependent), however, no changes were seen between dutasteride-treated versus vehicle-treated patients, indicating no androgen regulation of these genes in normal benign epithelial prostate cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2D and represents an inference from the lack of enrichment.

claim: Expression of the 452 gene signature was significantly and negatively enriched in CaP compared with benign prostate.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Tomlins et al., 2007; Heemers et al., 2011), expression of the 452 gene signature was significantly and negatively enriched in CaP compared with benign prostate.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2D and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The global 452 AR target gene set had a significant NES in biochemically recurring or metastatic CaP.
source: In each study, the global 452 AR target gene set had a significant NES in the most aggressive state (biochemically recurring or metastatic CaP) but one or more of the 17 coregulator-dependent subsignatures showed no enrichment between recurring and non-recurring CaPs or between localized CaP or CaP that had spread.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Consensus binding motifs for p53 were enriched selectively in ARBSs of WDR77-dependent AR target genes.
source: Consensus binding motifs for p53 were enriched selectively in ARBSs of WDR77-dependent AR target genes.
evidence: This is supported by cistrome analysis shown in Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: Five of 7 IPA-identified biological processes that associated significantly with the WDR77-dependent AR target genes were consistent with p53 function.
source: Five (cell death and DNA replication, recombination and repair) of 7 IPA-identified biological processes that associated significantly with the WDR77-dependent AR target genes were very consistent with p53 function (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on IPA functional analysis and known p53 functions.

claim: WDR77-dependent AR target genes included MYC, a well-known p53 target gene.
source: WDR77-dependent AR target genes included for instance MYC, a well-known p53 target gene with pivotal roles in CaP aggressiveness and progression.
evidence: This is supported by the gene list data and established knowledge about MYC as a p53 target.

claim: IPA identified p53 as an upstream regulator function of WDR77- and AR-regulated genes (p=1.37.e−7).
source: In addition, IPA identified p53 as an upstream regulator function of WDR77- and AR-regulated genes (p=1.37.e−7).
evidence: This is supported by IPA upstream regulator analysis.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation assays revealed that WDR77 and p53 are part of the same immune complex in LNCaP cells.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assays were done in both directions (i.e. immunoprecipitation for p53 and immunoblotting for WDR77, and immunoprecipitation for WDR77 followed by western blotting for p53) in LNCaP cells, which express wild-type p53. These studies revealed that WDR77 and p53 are part of the same immune complex (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: WDR77 and p53 are part of the same protein complex in VCaP cells.
source: These same experiments were performed in VCaP cells, which confirmed the presence of p53 and WDR77 in the same protein complex regardless of the order in which the immunoprecipitation or -blotting was done (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Androgen regulation of a set of 272 genes was affected similarly by knockdown of p53 or WDR77 (p<2.2E-16).
source: As shown in Figure 3F, androgen regulation of a set of 272 genes was affected similarly by knockdown of p53 or WDR77 (p<2.2E-16).
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 76.9% of genes for which androgen-responsiveness was increased after p53 knock-down overlapped with genes for which level of androgen-regulation was enhanced upon silencing of WDR77.
source: 76.9% of genes for which androgen-responsiveness was increased after p53 knock-down overlapped with genes for which level of androgen-regulation was enhanced upon silencing of WDR77.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data comparing p53 and WDR77 knockdown effects.

claim: 88.2% of genes for which androgen-responsiveness is enhanced after loss of WDR77 showed an increased level of androgen regulation also in p53 siRNA-transfected cells.
source: Conversely, 88.2% of genes for which androgen-responsiveness is enhanced after loss of WDR77 showed an increased level of androgen regulation also in p53 siRNA-transfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data comparing p53 and WDR77 knockdown effects.

claim: 68.3% of genes for which androgen-responsiveness decreased after loss of p53 overlapped with genes for which level of androgen-regulation was diminished upon silencing of WDR77.
source: Similarly, 68.3% of genes for which androgen-responsiveness decreased after loss of p53 overlapped with genes for which level of androgen-regulation was diminished upon silencing of WDR77
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data comparing p53 and WDR77 knockdown effects.

claim: 67% of genes for which level of androgen-responsiveness was lessened after loss of WDR77 showed decreased androgen regulation also in p53 siRNA transfection condition.
source: and 67% of genes for which level of androgen-responsiveness was lessened after loss of WDR77 showed decreased androgen regulation also in p53 siRNA transfection condition.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data comparing p53 and WDR77 knockdown effects.

claim: For none of the androgen-regulated genes isolated, inconsistency in the directionality of androgen regulation was observed between p53 and WDR77 silencing.
source: For none of the androgen-regulated genes isolated, inconsistency in the directionality of androgen regulation was observed between p53 and WDR77 silencing.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data comparing p53 and WDR77 knockdown effects.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation validated STAT3 and IRF1 interaction.
source: The ability of cistrome data to predict TF-coregulator interactions was validated by co-immuoprecipitation of STAT3 and IRF1, for which binding sites are enriched selectively in the ARBSs of STAT3- dependent genes (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experimental data in Supplementary file 6.

claim: Considerable overlap (n = 413) in androgen-responsive genes exists between IRF1 and STAT3 silencing (p<2.2E-16).
source: Gene expression studies following siRNA-mediated silencing of IRF1 and STAT3 confirmed considerable (n = 413) overlap in androgen-responsive genes (p<2.2E-16) (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis after IRF1 and STAT3 knockdown in Supplementary file 6.

claim: The directionality of androgen regulation of affected genes was preserved in IRF1- or STAT3-knockdown condition.
source: The directionality of androgen regulation of affected genes was preserved in IRF1- or STAT3-knockdown condition.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis in Supplementary file 6.

claim: Recent NextGen sequencing studies have identified p53 mutants that are enriched in castration-recurrent CaP.
source: Recent NextGen sequencing studies have identified p53 mutants that are enriched in castration-recurrent (CR-)CaP, but the contribution of these p53 mutants to AR-dependent transcription is poorly understood (Cronauer et al., 2004; Shenk et al., 2001; Gurova et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent sequencing studies.

claim: VCaP cells endogenously express gain-of-function p53 R248Q.
source: WDR77 and p53 were part of the same immunocomplex in VCaP cells (Figure 3D–E) that endogenously express gain-of-function p53 R248Q.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the VCaP cell line.

claim: Higher nuclear expression level of p53 mutants than wild-type p53 was observed in LNCaP cells.
source: Higher nuclear expression level of p53 mutants than wild-type p53 was observed, which is reminiscent of observations in patient specimens (Haffner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Increased p53 nuclear expression did not impact on nuclear content of AR or WDR77.
source: Increased p53 nuclear expression did not impact on nuclear content of AR or WDR77 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overall androgen regulation of GNB4 and RAB27A was maintained in the presence of added mutant p53.
source: Despite some heterogeneity in the contribution of different p53 mutants, overall androgen regulation of GNB4 and RAB27A was maintained in the presence of added mutant p53 (modeling clinically relevant heterotetramerization between wild-type and mutant p53 (e.g. [Muller and Vousden, 2014]), compared to empty vector or wild-type p53 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-IP studies confirmed interaction of mutant p53 (C135Y and N239T) with WDR77.
source: Co-IP studies in which 2 representative p53 mutants, C135Y and N239T, were expressed in a p53-null LNCaP subline (Guseva et al., 2012) confirmed interaction of mutant p53 with WDR77 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IP-mass-spectrometry analysis identified 3 proteins (14-3-3 sigma, hnRNPU and PGAM5) as part of the AR-WDR77-p53 immunocomplex.
source: IP-mass-spectrometry analysis was performed on nuclear fractions from androgen- versus vehicle-treated LNCaP cells. IP experiments in which either p53 or WDR77 antibodies were used independently identified 3 proteins (14-3-3 sigma, hnRNPU and PGAM5) as part of the AR-WDR77-p53 immunocomplex.
evidence: This is supported by IP-mass spectrometry experimental data.

claim: Expression of PGAM5 was significantly higher in CaP than in benign prostate (score of 2.24 vs 1.58, p=0.00059).
source: Expression of PGAM5 was significantly higher in CaP than in benign prostate (score of 2.24 vs 1.58, p=0.00059, t-test) and was higher also in CaPs of Gleason scores 7–10 than in CaP of Gleason score 6 (p<0.05, t-test) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data on tissue microarrays shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: PGAM5 expression was higher in CaPs of Gleason scores 7–10 than in CaP of Gleason score 6 (p<0.05).
source: Expression of PGAM5 was significantly higher in CaP than in benign prostate (score of 2.24 vs 1.58, p=0.00059, t-test) and was higher also in CaPs of Gleason scores 7–10 than in CaP of Gleason score 6 (p<0.05, t-test) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Oncomine and cBioPortal databases indicated overexpression of PGAM5 in CaP versus benign prostate.
source: These findings were in line with queries of the Oncomine and cBioPortal databases which indicated also overexpression of PGAM5 in CaP versus benign prostate, and increased PGAM5 expression with increasing Gleason grade and CaP progression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of public database data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PGAM5 expression increased with increasing Gleason grade and CaP progression.
source: These findings were in line with queries of the Oncomine and cBioPortal databases which indicated also overexpression of PGAM5 in CaP versus benign prostate, and increased PGAM5 expression with increasing Gleason grade and CaP progression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of public database data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PGAM5 exists in 2 isoforms (long and short).
source: PGAM5 exists in 2 isoforms (long and short).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGAM5 protein structure.

claim: Both PGAM5 forms are present in the AR-WDR77-p53 complex in LNCaP cells.
source: Co-IPs using antibodies directed against AR or p53 for IP confirmed the presence of both PGAM5 forms in the AR-WDR77-p53 complex in LNCaP cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Androgen treatment induced recruitment of PGAM5 and p53 to ARE-containing regions within GNB4 and RAB27A genes.
source: Androgen treatment induced recruitment of PGAM5 as well as p53 to ARE-containing regions within the genes encoding GNB4 and RAB27A, to which WDR77 and AR also bind (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Knock-down of PGAM5 mirrored the effect of WDR77 loss on androgen regulation of RAB27A and GNB4.
source: Knock-down of PGAM5 mirrored the effect of WDR77 loss on androgen regulation of target genes such as RAB27A and GNB4.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis after PGAM5 knockdown.

claim: Loss of PGAM5 altered the androgen responsiveness of 218/272 of the p53 and WDR77-dependent genes (p<2.2E-16).
source: Genome-wide oligoarray expression profiling in LNCaP cells showed that loss of PGAM5 altered the androgen responsiveness of 218/272 of the p53 and WDR77-dependent genes (p<2.2E-16) (Figure 5G), and for each of those genes the impact on directionality of androgen regulation was the same for PGAM5 loss as that observed after silencing of WDR77 and p53.
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: For genes affected by PGAM5 loss, the impact on directionality of androgen regulation was the same as that observed after silencing of WDR77 and p53.
source: Genome-wide oligoarray expression profiling in LNCaP cells showed that loss of PGAM5 altered the androgen responsiveness of 218/272 of the p53 and WDR77-dependent genes (p<2.2E-16) (Figure 5G), and for each of those genes the impact on directionality of androgen regulation was the same for PGAM5 loss as that observed after silencing of WDR77 and p53.
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Loss of WDR77 altered androgen-dependent pattern of coimmunoprecipitation of p53 by AR.
source: At the molecular level, loss of WDR77 altered androgen-dependent pattern of coimmunoprecipitation of p53 by AR (Figure 5H), and silencing of either WDR77 or PGAM5 prevented androgen-dependent recruitment of p53 to WDR77-dependent target genes (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Silencing of either WDR77 or PGAM5 prevented androgen-dependent recruitment of p53 to WDR77-dependent target genes.
source: At the molecular level, loss of WDR77 altered androgen-dependent pattern of coimmunoprecipitation of p53 by AR (Figure 5H), and silencing of either WDR77 or PGAM5 prevented androgen-dependent recruitment of p53 to WDR77-dependent target genes (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: ChIP-re-ChIP experiments confirmed androgen-stimulated co-recruitment of AR and p53 to GNB4 and RAB27A genes, which was decreased following siRNA-mediated silencing of WDR77.
source: Moreover, ChIP-re-ChIP expertiments using an antibody targeting p53 for ChIP and an antibody against AR for Re-ChIP confirmed androgen-stimulated co-recruitment of AR and p53 to these genes, which was decreased following siRNA-mediated silencing of WDR77. Similar results were obtained in parallel experiments in which ChIP targeted AR and Re-ChIP was directed at p53 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-re-ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of WDR77, PGAM5, HES6, AGR2, GNB4 and RAB27A markedly reduced cell viability of LNCaP cells under normal culture conditions.
source: siRNA-mediated silencing of all regulators and target genes markedly reduced cell viability of LNCaP cells, both under normal culture conditions and under androgen-stimulated conditions (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by MTS cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of WDR77, PGAM5, HES6, AGR2, GNB4 and RAB27A markedly reduced cell viability of LNCaP cells under androgen-stimulated conditions.
source: siRNA-mediated silencing of all regulators and target genes markedly reduced cell viability of LNCaP cells, both under normal culture conditions and under androgen-stimulated conditions (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by MTS cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Similar effects on cell viability were observed in p53-null LNCaP sublines that are stably transfected with expression constructs encoding p53 mutants C135Y and N239T.
source: Similar effects were observed when experiments were repeated in p53-null LNCaP sublines that are stably transfected with expression constructs encoding p53 mutants C135Y and N239T or in VCaP cells that express p53 R248Q (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Similar effects on cell viability were observed in VCaP cells that express p53 R248Q.
source: Similar effects were observed when experiments were repeated in p53-null LNCaP sublines that are stably transfected with expression constructs encoding p53 mutants C135Y and N239T or in VCaP cells that express p53 R248Q (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Propidium iodide FACS studies indicated that reduced cell viability may be due to slow G1 phase progression and G1/S transition.
source: Except for GNB4, for which effects were modest, propidium iodide FACS studies in LNCaP cells indicated that this reduced cell viability may be due to slow G1 phase progression and G1/S transition (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6E and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Western blot analysis showed marked increases in expression of gamma-pH2AX after silencing of regulators and effectors of the AR-WDR77-p53 transcriptional code.
source: Western blot analysis on parallel samples showed marked increases in expression of gamma-pH2AX, supporting potential effects on cell cycle stage, early apoptosis and/or DNA damage (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: AR and p53 have never been found to interact directly despite previous reports of functional interaction.
source: Despite previous reports of functional interaction between AR and p53 (Dean and Knudsen, 2013; Guseva et al., 2012; Cronauer et al., 2004; Shenk et al., 2001; Gurova et al., 2002), these proteins have never been found to interact directly.
evidence: This is based on a review of literature as indicated by the citations.

claim: Interaction between WDR77 and AR has been described.
source: However, interaction between WDR77 and AR has been described (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: p53 mutations are present in >50% of CR-CaP cases.
source: p53 mutations are present in >50% of CR-CaP cases.
evidence: This is established knowledge from clinical sequencing studies.

claim: WDR77 is expressed in clinical CR-CaP.
source: WDR77 is expressed also in clinical CR-CaP (Peng et al., 2008), and our data indicate that interaction between WDR77 and mutant p53 is maintained.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2008 and experimental data from this study.

claim: Interaction between WDR77 and mutant p53 is maintained.
source: WDR77 is expressed also in clinical CR-CaP (Peng et al., 2008), and our data indicate that interaction between WDR77 and mutant p53 is maintained.
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PGAM5 has previously been reported to play a role in regulation of cell death.
source: PGAM5, which has previously been reported to play a role in regulation of cell death (Vaseva et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012) but was not known to be relevant to AR signaling or CaP biology, was prioritized for validation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vaseva et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2012.

claim: PGAM5 was not known to be relevant to AR signaling or CaP biology prior to this study.
source: PGAM5, which has previously been reported to play a role in regulation of cell death (Vaseva et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012) but was not known to be relevant to AR signaling or CaP biology, was prioritized for validation.
evidence: This represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.
